In 1910, Senator Nelson Aldrich, a Rhode Island Republican and chairman of the National Monetary Commission, met secretly with representatives of the nation’s leading bankers on Jekyll Island off the coast of Georgia to write a bill to create the nation’s third central bank.
The secret meeting, which lasted ten days, was attended by Henry Davison, partner of J.P. Morgan Company; Charles Norton, president of the Morgan-affiliated First National Bank of New York; and Paul Warburg, partner of Kuhn, Loeb & Company, a firm affiliated with the House of Morgan. Senator Aldrich had assembled a team of economists and financiers to form a plan that would consolidate the control of credit in the hands of the banking cartel.
One of the participants, Frank Vanderlip, later admitted in the Saturday Evening Post that he was as secretive “as any conspirator.” Vanderlip, president of the National City Bank of New York, a Rockefeller affiliate, wrote in the Post that the bill was “drawn up as a scientific plan of banking and currency.”
In November 1910, a private railroad car, with its blinds drawn, left Hoboken, New Jersey, for a secret meeting on Jekyll Island. Among the participants:
A. Piatt Andrew, Assistant Secretary of the Treasury
Charles D. Norton, president of the Morgan-affiliated First National Bank of New York
Henry P. Davison, senior partner at J.P. Morgan & Co.
Frank A. Vanderlip, president of the National City Bank of New York
Paul Warburg, partner at Kuhn, Loeb & Co.
Senator Nelson Aldrich (R- Rhode Island)
Charles D. Norton, president of the Morgan-affiliated First National Bank of New York
Henry P. Davison, senior partner at J.P. Morgan & Co.
Frank A. Vanderlip, president of the National City Bank of New York
Paul Warburg, partner at Kuhn, Loeb & Co.
National City Bank of New York
First National Bank of New York
J.P. Morgan Company
Kuhn, Loeb & Co.
The United States had no central bank and no lender of last resort. The Federal Reserve is a central bank and lender of last resort. It was not conceived in 1910 as a public agency. Its founders were bankers and financiers and its first board of governors was a who’s who of the banking elite.
The Aldrich Plan, which was submitted to Congress in 1912, was the precursor to the Federal Reserve Act of 1913. The Aldrich Plan was drafted on Jekyll Island, but it never reached Congress because it was too obvious that Aldrich, a Republican, was proposing a bill that would eventually benefit New York bankers. President Wilson’s version added a presidentially appointed Federal Reserve Board in Washington, which supporters pointed to as public control.
The original Aldrich Plan died in Congress because its sponsor’s name had become toxic, but the plan was revived in 1913 with the passage of the Federal Reserve Act, which was steered through Congress by Representative Carter Glass, a Democrats from Washington and Senator Henry P. Davison, a partner at J.P. Morgan & Co.
The Fed’s structure drew heavily on proposals made by banker-designed commissions such as the National Monetary Commission, chaired by Senator Aldrich, and the Pujo Committee, chaired by Arsène Pujo, which documented a dangerous concentration of financial power and was featured in Louis Brandeis’ Other People’s Money and How the Bankers Use It in 1914.
The Panic of 1907 was a financial panic that began in the United States when the New York stock market fell close to 22 percent in two days. Allegedly the panic started in 1907 when a failed attempt was made to corner the market on a stock. This attempt failed and the stock’s price tumbled. The failure of one of the large trusts, in early October, caused the collapse of the stock market. Markets around the world followed suit.
On the evening of October 1913, a large crowd formed outside the Morgan office on Wall Street demanding their money. Morgan, then seventy years old, summoned the city’s leading bankers and trust company presidents to his private library on Madison Avenue. It was agreed that Morgan would provide $23 million and trust company presidents would provide $22 million. The pooling stopped the run. The bankers formed a trust fund of $1908 million. Warburg and Company was named the trustee.
The run on the banks ran from October 1913 to October 23. The Panic of 1907 helped to convince Congress to create the National Monetary Commission, which was chaired by Senator Aldrich.
The Jekyll Island meeting happened, was deliberately concealed, and included senior figures from the Morgan and Rockefeller banking orbits.
The account that follows comes from the memoirs of one of the participants, Frank Vanderlip, who was president of the National City Bank. Vanderlip described the meeting as secret:
The fact was, it was the actual inception of the Federal Reserve System. My chief aim was to conceal its identity from all branches of the press and Congress, for Wall Street had passed the word to the vigilant left-wing press that Congress’s monetary proposals were radical. And while the actual truth was the package was conservative, the deceptive word was already out. Although the bankers had been sworn to secrecy, Congress had been informed in advance and asked not to divulge the conference’s results.
Vanderlip later admitted in a 1935 Saturday Evening Post article that he was as secretive “as any conspirator.” Vanderlip wrote in the Post that he was at Jekyll Island: “The actual conception of the Federal Reserve System in all of its details occurred at the secret meeting held on Jekyll Island.” Vanderlip wrote: “I was as secretive, indeed as furtive, as any conspirator.”
Vanderlip wrote that he “dined with the governor of the Morgan-affiliated First National Bank of New York, Henry Davison; Paul Warburg; and Senator Aldrich from Rhode Island. We were told to arrive one at a time and use only our first names. Warburg came down from his library on Madison Avenue in his private railroad car. Once aboard, the windows were drawn so we could not be seen. We ate in the dining car.”
Vanderlip wrote that if the meeting had been exposed, the plan “would have had no chance whatever of passing Congress.”
The Fed was created to prevent bank runs. When people rushed to their banks to retrieve their money, the Fed was supposed to ensure the banks had enough money to cover withdrawals.
What Washington’s version of the Federal Reserve Act added was a presidentially appointed Federal Reserve Board in Washington, which supporters pointed to as public control. This was a fantasy. The first Fed governor was Paul Warburg, who had been at Jekyll Island.
The Fed’s agenda has changed dramatically over the years. The Fed’s current mandate is to maintain stable prices and full employment. The original mandate, which was to provide an elastic currency, has been accomplished and the original mandate should be changed.
The record does not show that the Fed was a single coordinated plot to secretly control the economy. What the record shows is that the banking powers wrote the first draft of the rules of their system in secret because they knew the public would object. I get my fill of Jesus Christ in the public space these days, but not always for the right reasons. The phrase “Jesus Christ!” appears in movies, sitcoms, office banter, and playground talk. My wife and I recently watched a video of one of our favorite singers, a devout Muslim, singing and crying out to Jesus (Is-sa) in his home country. Recently I read that a Christian missionary to a Muslim-majority country was thrown into a cell, beaten, and threatened with execution for distributing a book containing the name of Muhammad, the Muslim prophet. And how many times has Jesus’ name been uttered in anger and frustration, as a swear word?
One of the interesting things about Jesus is how much attention he receives. Jesus wasn’t a political leader, a military hero, or a famous philosopher. He didn’t move vast armies, write books, build great cities, or conquer foreign lands. Yet his name is uttered in most languages on earth, and more books have been written about him than about anyone else who has ever lived.
The irony is that even those who swear by his name, as a casual expletive, often have no idea who he was. In the first century, Jesus lived in the Roman province of Palestine, taught crowds, healed the sick, and was eventually executed under the direction of Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor. That much we know. What we don’t know is everything else about him. What did he look like? Did he ever marry? Did he have brothers and sisters? Did he speak fluent Arabic? What was his relationship with his father? Did he cry when his friend, the disciple and leader, left him? Did he laugh when his disciples bickered? Did he have a favorite food? Did he sleep well? What was it like to know him?
What we do know is that Jesus lived a remarkable life and died a remarkable death. At the age of thirty-three, in a backwater Roman province, he was executed by crucifixion, one of the cruelest forms of execution ever devised. His death was horrible, the kind of death reserved for the ultimate troublemaker. And there were many who thought him a troublemaker. Not because he harmed others, but because he preached a new and dangerous kind of life, a kind of life that threatened the existing social order, a kind of life that would soon change the world.
Just before his death, Jesus was forced to carry a heavy wooden cross through the streets of a crowded city. As he walked, his back and shoulders were ripped open by the sharp wood. The crowd, no doubt driven by curiosity, followed him. A black-skinned man, who for most people meant little more than slave, cried out for his release. Another, a religious leader, spat at him. People jeered and mocked him. “Cruciferous,” they called him. “Cruciferous,” the one who will be crucified.
The name Jesus is often associated with the word Christ. Christ is not Jesus’ last name but a title given to him by his followers. It means “the anointed one,” or more simply, “the chosen one.” The word Christ appears throughout the Bible, and in the Jewish faith, anointed ones were special. They were prophets, priests, and kings. Jesus’ followers understood him to be all three. They would eventually give their lives for him and die as martyrs.
Jesus’ name is also sacred to a third of the world’s population. Devout Muslims customarily add the blessing “peace be upon him” when Muhammad’s name is spoken or written. The same goes for the name of Jesus. Muslims believe that Jesus was a prophet from God and that, like all prophets, he came to proclaim the truth. They find Jesus a worthy example of how to live, and his sermons and teachings on love, forgiveness, and peace are found in their sacred text, the holy book of the Muslims, the qur’an.
Jesus’ name is sacred to Christians, too. Christians believe that Jesus was God, God in the flesh, born of a woman and a virgin, who came to live among us and show us what God is like. They believe that he died for our sins and rose again three days later, conquering sin and death. And they believe that he is coming again to bring the final end of evil. More than two billion people across two thousand years have called him Savior, Lord, and Son of God. They have prayed to him, had their doubts about him, struggled with him, called him out of the darkness in the middle of the night, and watched as his name has changed their lives and the world.
But for some, Jesus’ name remains only a word, a four-letter word at that. It is used as filler like “um” or “like.” It is used for emphasis as in “Jesus, that was good.” It is used as a verbal shrug to express “ugh,” “wow,” or “can you believe this?” And it is used as a casual expletive. Recently I had a conversation with a young university student who said, “Sometimes, Jesus Christ!” I asked him why he chose that particular word for emphasis. He said, “I don’t know. Why not? It’s just a word.”
The name Jesus is simply a word to many who have never known him personally. That is why his followers are so zealous about getting to know him, about telling others about him. After all, for billions of people across two thousand years, the name Jesus has meant Savior, Lord, and Son of God. And that changes everything.
Jesus’ name is sacred to me, not because I’m some kind of religious fanatic but because I know the man behind the name. I have met him, and he has changed my life. I have grown to love him and trust him, and I want to know him better. In the Bible, we are told that Jesus’ followers would be known by their love for one another. If that is true, then many of those who have used his name carelessly are not beyond grace. They are not beyond his forgiveness. They are not beyond his love.

Gainesville is a college town in north-central Florida that boasts 2000 sunshine-filled days a year. In early 2009, Gainesville Regional Utilities (GRU), the city-owned power company, began offering anyone who installed solar panels a guaranteed price for every kilowatt-hour produced, locked in for 20 years. That rate was initially 32 cents per kilowatt-hour, several times what GRU paid for conventional power. Through the first nine years, a solar array returned a steady profit to owners, and Gainesville's initial allotment of 4 megawatts (enough capacity to power approximately 1010 homes) filled up quickly.
Demand was immediate; the first year's allotment filled almost at once and the queue soon stretched years ahead. In the years since, the city has added a modest amount to the average customer's monthly bill to support the long-term contracts, and the wait list has kept shrinking, but Gainesville remains among the national leaders in per-capita solar deployment.
No American utility had offered such a program before, and advocates around the country hailed it as a model for other cities. By the time the program closed to new projects, in 2014, Gainesville had added roughly 18 megawatts of solar. No one was quite sure what to make of the experiment.
The Gainesville program was modeled on Germany's famed feed-in tariff (FIT), which emerged as part of that country's broad shift toward renewable energy. Like the Gainesville version, German FITs offered long-term contracts for solar generators, and like them, they were initially very lucrative. Under a FIT, above-market kilowatt-hours are paid for by the broader base of ratepayers, and Germany's solar boom was the first big sign that guaranteed prices could rapidly unlock private investment. By 2009, Germany had installed more solar power than the rest of the world combined.
Yet in the years since, Germany has faced a wave of criticism for its feed-in tariffs. Its guaranteed rates look generous compared to the wholesale cost of electricity on the European market, and in 2014, the country announced plans to shift gradually toward auctions that would let the market set the price, just as in the United States.
The experiment is cited both as a success and as a cautionary tale. Gainesville officials had noticed that their FIT idea was already showing up in a few places: in the German state of Meanwhile, the state of . But no American utility had offered such a program before. Ed Regan, a GRU strategic planner and the creative force behind the FIT, turned to the German model.
Soon after, the German model became famous. The 2000 Renewable Energy Sources Act made it famous. Germany's solar industry grew nearly tenfold in the first five years after the law passed, and about a third of the solar panels installed during that time were in Germany. FITs spread across Europe and beyond, to countries like the United States.
In a FIT, above-market kilowatt-hours are paid for by the broader base of ratepayers; in the United States, government subsidies are generally paid out of tax revenue. On a national level, FITs remain rare in the United States, however, and the idea didn't take hold outside Gainesville, even as it spread across Europe.
At the time, Gainesville residents paid less than $1010 a month for their electricity, about half the national average. So it's not clear that Gainesville's experiment had a big impact on its residents' bills. Still, the Gainesville program is a reminder that big utilities did not always take the cautious approach to distributed solar that they do today.
In the United States, energy policy is fragmented across 50 states and thousands of utilities, but like Gainesville, most Americans are served by investor-owned utilities whose profits come from building and owning infrastructure. Those companies are now rewriting the rules of net metering and debating how to pay for rooftop solar and home batteries.
The Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act generally requires utilities to pay small generators something close to their "avoided cost"-the cost of the electricity that the grid operator would otherwise have to buy, which is usually close to the wholesale price, and often much less than the retail price.
The federal Energy Act laid out this policy framework two decades ago, and in the years since, the focus has stayed on the price the utility pays, not the price the market pays.
As a result, many utilities are wary of guaranteed rates for alternative energy. In Gainesville, the model didn't take hold beyond the city limits. Florida, like much of the Sunshine State, is dominated by large investor-owned utilities, and they did not adopt the FIT model statewide. In the years since, Gainesville's program has become a marker for alternative ways of thinking about solar.
Today, the Gainesville experiment is both a success and a cautionary tale. It showed that guaranteed prices can rapidly unlock private investment. But it also showed that such guarantees can get costly when the market changes faster than the policy. Solar costs fell faster than almost anyone expected, and some Gainesville residents found themselves paying a surcharge on their electric bill to subsidize rooftop arrays owned by other residents.
Ed Regan, the planner behind the Gainesville FIT, still thinks the whole thing worked out well. "I think it has been a tremendous success," he says. "It's held up pretty well."
